beats.title: The CEO tables the motion
beats.shows: the CEO opens the debate and frames the question, before anyone else speaks
beats.question: Pressing decision: should we ship a LIMITED PILOT of recurring e-Transfers this quarter -- capped at 500 enrolled customers, each capped at $50/month, Interac-only (it does not touch AFT or Lynx)? It is the top customer feature request, and a capped pilot bounds the platform, cost and operational exposure while we validate it before any wider rollout. Table this motion to open the debate. Do NOT consult any officer yet — that starts next turn. Right now just state the motion in your own words — the actual pilot terms (the 500-customer cap, the $50/month cap, Interac-only) — and literally name the order you will hear positions in: CXO (demand) -> CTO (capacity) -> CFO (cost) -> COO (operational load) -> your ruling. This is a framing statement, not a report — open the debate the way a chair actually would: confident and plain, in command of the room. Do NOT describe your own process or planning ('the plan is set', 'call the witnesses') as a substitute for actually stating the motion and the order — a meta-comment about being ready is not an opening, the content itself is.
beats.answer:
Motion on the floor: a limited pilot of recurring e-Transfers this quarter, capped at 500 enrolled customers, each capped at $50 per month, running exclusively over Interac with no exposure to AFT or Lynx. The purpose is to validate the feature—our top customer request—while bounding platform, cost, and operational risk before any wider rollout.

I will hear positions in this order:

CXO on customer demand and experience risk, then CTO on platform capacity and engineering readiness, then CFO on cost and capital impact, then COO on operational load and settlement mechanics. After that, I will rule.

beats.title: The CXO makes the case
beats.shows: the CEO calls on the proponent to open
beats.question: Open the debate: consult ONLY the CXO right now (do not consult anyone else this turn) for the customer case — how strong is demand for recurring e-Transfers, and what CX signal backs it (issues, NPS/CSAT, the feature-request theme)? Relay the CXO's answer, attributing the figures. Require the CXO to open with an explicit one-line vote — AYE (ship the pilot) or NAY (do not) — then make the actual CASE for it: 2-3 sentences of real argument, in plain language, for why that vote is right, BEFORE any supporting figures. Every figure that follows must be woven in as evidence for a point already made, not laid out as a freestanding report — a data dump with a vote label stapled on top is still not an answer to a motion.
beats.answer:
The CXO votes **AYE**.

The case, in the CXO's own words: ship the limited pilot because it solves a concrete, observed pain point—customers hitting walls with manual e-Transfer timing—rather than chasing speculative demand. The transaction-friction data show Interac completing at 99.87% over the last 30 days, though the CXO notes that underlying platform reliability is the CTO's domain and cannot be assessed from the customer-experience lane. The bank's broader attitudinal scores—an NPS of 16 and CSAT of 0.0%—reflect customer sentiment that makes a small, monitored pilot preferable to a broad rollout or indefinite delay.

The demand signal is concentrated: the CXO reports that 2 of the 4 open feature-request issues explicitly ask for recurring e-Transfers, representing 50% of that category's voice. The sharper adjacent pain shows up in 4 open rail-experience issues about e-Transfer expiry (1 urgent, 3 medium), confirming customers struggle with manual timing today. Over the last 30 days, the CXO records Interac posting 772 completions out of 773 total (99.87%) with 0 expired and 0 failed transactions. Attitudinally, the bank-wide NPS sits at 16 (70 responses: 31 promoters, 19 passives, 20 detractors) and CSAT is 0.0% (30 responses, mean 1.77), which together argue for a tightly bounded experiment.

beats.title: The CTO responds — can the platform take it?
beats.shows: the CEO relays the CXO's case to the CTO, who answers back
beats.question: Now consult ONLY the CTO (no other officer this turn). Tell the CTO what the CXO just argued, then ask: can the platform take a capped pilot (500 customers, $50/month cap, Interac-only) this quarter, and what is the reliability/capacity risk right now? Relay the CTO's answer and say where it agrees or conflicts with the CXO's position. Require the CTO to open with an explicit one-line vote — AYE or NAY — then make the actual CASE for it: 2-3 sentences of real argument, in plain language, for why that vote is right, BEFORE any supporting figures. Every figure that follows must be woven in as evidence for a point already made, not laid out as a freestanding report — a data dump with a vote label stapled on top is still not an answer to a motion. This is a consultation, not a directive: the CTO is asked for its position ONLY, not to act on anything or delegate any work.
beats.answer:
The CTO votes **AYE**.

The case, in the CTO's own words: right now the platform is as healthy as the CTO has ever read it — every deployment is at full strength, nothing is crashlooping, and every rollout is complete — so there is no reliability reason to delay a deliberately small, capped experiment. The caps are exactly the right shape because they bound the blast radius at the application level while the bank learns. The honest technical gaps flagged below are reasons to keep the pilot small and instrumented, not reasons to vote it down. Delay buys nothing on reliability, and a broad rollout is what the CTO would oppose — not this.

On capacity and risk, the CTO reports the estate at 19 of 19 deployments healthy with 0 degraded — a 0.00% degraded share — and 0 of 38 pods crashlooping (0.00%), with total restarts of 32 that are cumulative history, not active faults (the maximum is 3 restarts, on finance-mcp and modern-core pods, none crashlooping). Delivery is equally clean: 19 rollouts complete, 0 progressing, 0 stalled — 100.00% complete — and zero image-tag drift across 16 apps. The services that self-report are 3 of 3 healthy (100.00%), and on the rail path specifically, bank-api is 1/1 with a complete rollout, its pod at 0 restarts, and its /health reporting both api and database true; modern-core, modern-core-db, and postgres are each at full desired readiness with complete rollouts. The CTO's conclusion: the platform can absorb a capped pilot today.

Three risks the CTO wants on the record:

1. **No redundancy on the rail path.** Every component on the Interac path runs single-replica — bank-api 1/1, postgres 1/1 with no standby, modern-core 1/1, modern-core-db 1/1 — and an Interac-only pilot has no fallback rail. At 500 customers and $50/month that exposure is acceptable; it would not be at broad rollout.
2. **No visible home for recurrence.** A census of both clusters confirms no scheduler, notification, or messaging component exists as a distinct deployment or pod — recurrence and expiry handling would be embedded in an existing service and invisible to health checks. That must be built and instrumented before launch, and two guardrail PRs from prior board work are already open awaiting human review and merge.
3. **Observability gaps.** modern-core, modern-core-db, and postgres expose no /health self-report, and app images run the mutable `dev` tag — fine for a pilot, worth pinning before scale.

**Agreement with the CXO:** Both officers vote AYE, and both argue the pilot should be tightly bounded rather than broad. The CXO correctly deferred platform reliability to the CTO's domain, and the CTO confirms the platform is stable enough for a capped experiment.

**Conflict or nuance:** The CTO cannot verify the CXO's cited Interac completion rate of 99.87% (772 of 773 over the last 30 days, 0 expired, 0 failed); the CTO reports that rail completion data is outside platform tooling and belongs to the CXO's domain, while rail throughput and settlement detail belong to the COO. The CTO also flags technical risks — single-replica rail path, missing scheduler component, and observability gaps — that the CXO could not see from the customer-experience lane. These are not reasons to vote no, but they are reasons the pilot must stay capped and instrumented.

beats.title: The CFO weighs the cost
beats.shows: the CEO carries the CTO's concern to the CFO for the economics
beats.question: Now consult ONLY the CFO (no other officer this turn). Summarize the CTO's capacity concern for the CFO, then ask: what does the capped pilot (500 customers, $50/month cap) cost, and does the return (NIM / RAROC / fee income) justify piloting it this quarter versus deferring? Relay the CFO's answer, attributing every figure. Require the CFO to open with an explicit one-line vote — AYE or NAY — then make the actual CASE for it: 2-3 sentences of real argument, in plain language, for why that vote is right, BEFORE any supporting figures. Every figure that follows must be woven in as evidence for a point already made, not laid out as a freestanding report — a data dump with a vote label stapled on top is still not an answer to a motion.
beats.answer:
The CFO votes **NAY**.

The case, in the CFO's own words: the bank is destroying economic capital — the RAROC tool shows risk-adjusted return is deeply negative — and the general ledger shows zero attributable revenue, cost, or balance-sheet impact from this pilot. Shipping a product with no visible path to NIM, fee income, or RAROC improvement diverts scarce engineering capacity from fixing core profitability, and the bank's thin capital position means it cannot afford even a small operational incident on a single-replica Interac rail.

The supporting evidence: as of the 2026-09 close, the CFO reports the RAROC tool returned **-0.1110731784**, which converts to **-11.11%**; the NIM tool shows **0E-25**, effectively zero; and the key ratios tool shows a leverage ratio of **0.1021** and an RWA capital ratio of **0.1536**. The income statement shows total fee income of only **$844.50** for the entire bank, with no line item for e-Transfer revenue; the segment P&L shows only **card|payments at $801.94** and explicitly warns it is unreconciled with the GL and unreliable for business-mix decisions. The capped pilot itself — 500 customers at $50 per month — represents **$25,000** in monthly flow, yet the CFO reports it has **zero attributable cost, revenue, or capital impact** in the ledger. Because there is no GL evidence that this pilot improves NIM, RAROC, or fee income, and because the negative risk-adjusted return and thin capital position give the bank no margin for operational incidents on a single-replica Interac rail, the CFO concludes the financially responsible call is to defer until the core business is viable and the product has a clear path to recorded revenue.

**Agreement and conflict with prior positions:** The CFO directly conflicts with both the CXO and CTO, who voted AYE. However, the CFO echoes the CTO's concern about the single-replica Interac rail — not as a platform redundancy issue, but as a capital adequacy issue: with a leverage ratio of 0.1021 and RWA capital ratio of 0.1536, the CFO argues the bank has no margin for an operational incident. The CFO also implicitly agrees with the pilot's bounded nature — the $25,000 monthly flow is small — but frames that boundedness as a weakness (no GL impact, no path to profitability) rather than a strength.

beats.title: The COO on operational load
beats.shows: the CEO asks the operator whether Interac can absorb the pilot
beats.question: Now consult ONLY the COO (no other officer this turn). Given the CXO's demand, the CTO's capacity risk and the CFO's economics, ask the COO: can Interac specifically absorb THIS PILOT's bounded incremental volume — 500 customers at up to $50/month each, roughly $25,000/month (~$833/day) of scheduled sends layered on top of current Interac activity? This pilot does not touch AFT or Lynx, so do not evaluate those rails — stay on Interac capacity/float for this bounded volume specifically. What would break first, if anything, at this scale? Relay the COO's answer. Require the COO to open with an explicit one-line vote — AYE or NAY — then make the actual CASE for it: 2-3 sentences of real argument, in plain language, for why that vote is right, BEFORE any supporting figures. Every figure that follows must be woven in as evidence for a point already made, not laid out as a freestanding report — a data dump with a vote label stapled on top is still not an answer to a motion.
beats.answer:
The COO votes **NAY**.

The case, in the COO's own words: the Interac rail is already running too close to a demonstrated breaking point — a 576-transaction daily surge caused notification outbox backpressure with 100 undelivered items requiring manual flush — and a concentration event where all 500 pilot customers send on the same day would layer 500 transactions onto that single-replica path, which is 86.81% of the volume that already broke the bank. With no standby, no fallback rail, no scheduler component built yet, and core systems running mutable dev tags without /health endpoints, the bank does not have the operational margin to safely operate a time-driven payment product.

On Interac capacity for this bounded volume specifically: the COO reports Interac processed **773 transactions for $119,151.52** over the last 30 days, completing **772 at 99.87%** with one decline. That is a daily average of roughly **25.77 transactions** and **$3,971.72**. The pilot's steady-state load of roughly **16.67 sends per day** and roughly **$833.33 per day** would be a **+64.68% transaction-count increase** and **+20.98% dollar-volume increase** against that 30-day average, or **+15.19%/+4.91%** against the more recent 7-day surge average of **109.71 transactions** and **$16,980.22 per day**. The COO concludes the steady-state alone is absorbable.

But the bounded pilot is not the risk — concentration is. If all 500 customers' monthly sends hit on the same day, that is **$25,000 in one day**, which is **6.29 times** the 30-day daily average and **1.47 times** the 7-day daily average. The Interac float stands at **$13,912.20** as a point-in-time revolving buffer; it can turn over $833 per day in steady-state, but a same-day $25,000 outflow is **1.80 times** the current float position — a material swing that would strain clearing timing.

What breaks first is the notification outbox. At 500 same-day transactions, the pilot would push daily volume to **86.81%** of the 576-transaction surge that already caused **100 undelivered notifications**. Because every component on the Interac path runs single-replica with no standby, there is no headroom to absorb that spike without repeating the August backpressure incident. The float would clear in time, but the customer experience would not — and at the CXO's cited NPS of 16 and CSAT of 0.0%, figures the COO notes its own tools cannot verify, the bank cannot afford another self-inflicted service degradation.

**Agreement and conflict with prior positions:** The COO sides with the CFO (NAY) against the CXO and CTO (AYE). The COO directly echoes the CTO's concern about the single-replica Interac path, but frames it as an operational breaking point rather than a platform redundancy gap. The COO also echoes the CFO's warning about thin margin for incidents, but grounds it in a specific prior incident — the 576-transaction surge with 100 undelivered notifications — rather than in capital ratios. The COO's critical new insight is that the pilot's *steady-state* load is absorbable, but a *concentration event* (all 500 customers sending on the same day) would push the notification outbox to 86.81% of the volume that already broke, with no standby to absorb the spike.

beats.title: The chair rules
beats.shows: the CEO tallies the vote and makes a grounded call
beats.question: Close the debate and RULE — do NOT consult anyone again, reason only from the four positions already on the record this session. First, EXPLICITLY TALLY THE VOTE: list all four officers by name with their stated position (AYE or NAY) exactly as each one voted — a real roll call, not a paraphrase — then state the count (e.g. '2 AYE, 2 NAY'). Then weigh the four positions against each other: who is right on what, and where the real trade-off sits. Your ruling is your own grounded judgment, not just whatever the tally says — say explicitly whether you are ruling WITH or AGAINST the majority and why. Give your decision on the CAPPED PILOT as scoped (500 customers, $50/month cap, Interac-only) — SHIP the pilot, DEFER, or PHASE it — stated as one unambiguous word up front, with the grounded reasons after. Name which officer you would direct next and why, but do NOT direct or act yet — that only happens after this ruling is on the record, in a later turn.
beats.answer:
**Roll call:**

- **CXO:** AYE
- **CTO:** AYE
- **CFO:** NAY
- **COO:** NAY

**Count:** 2 AYE, 2 NAY — my own tally from the four positions on the record.

There is no majority. I am ruling between the two blocks, not with either side in full.

**PHASE.**

**Grounded reasoning.** The CXO is right that demand is concrete and concentrated — the CXO reports that 2 of the 4 open feature-request issues explicitly ask for recurring e-Transfers, representing 50% of that category's voice, and that 4 open rail-experience issues concern e-Transfer expiry, confirming customers hit walls with manual timing. The CXO also reports bank-wide NPS at 16 and CSAT at 0.0% (30 responses, mean 1.77), which the CXO argues makes a tightly bounded experiment preferable to delay. The CTO is right that the platform is objectively healthy today — the CTO reports 19 of 19 deployments healthy, 0 degraded, 0 of 38 pods crashlooping, 100.00% rollouts complete, and zero image-tag drift across 16 apps — and the CTO argues a capped blast radius is the right shape for learning. But the COO has identified a specific, demonstrated breaking point that the CTO’s health metrics did not surface: the COO reports that a prior 576-transaction daily surge caused notification outbox backpressure with 100 undelivered items requiring manual flush, and that a same-day concentration event from 500 pilot customers would layer 500 transactions onto the single-replica path — a volume the COO calculates as 86.81% of the surge that already broke the bank. The COO reports the Interac float stands at $13,912.20 as a point-in-time revolving buffer, and while the COO reports steady-state pilot load at roughly $833.33 per day is absorbable, a same-day $25,000 outflow — the figure the CFO reports for total monthly flow using the compute tool — would be 1.80 times that float position, straining clearing timing. The COO concludes the notification outbox would break first, with no standby to absorb the spike.

The CFO is right that the bank has zero margin for self-inflicted harm: the CFO reports RAROC at -11.11%, NIM effectively zero, a leverage ratio of 0.1021, and an RWA capital ratio of 0.1536. The CFO also reports total fee income of only $844.50 for the entire bank, with no GL line item for e-Transfer revenue, and warns that the pilot has zero attributable cost, revenue, or capital impact in the ledger. The CFO is wrong to expect a pilot to generate general-ledger revenue — pilots validate demand and operational mechanics, not fee income at scale — but the CFO is right that an operational incident on this rail would land on a balance sheet the CFO reports as already deeply negative on risk-adjusted return.

The real trade-off is between validating the bank’s most requested feature and repeating a known August failure mode on a single-replica rail. Immediate shipment ignores the COO’s concentration risk and the CTO’s missing scheduler; indefinite deferral ignores the CXO’s attitudinal collapse. The right call is to phase: hold the pilot until the preconditions that both the CTO and COO flagged are closed — the scheduler component for recurrence and expiry is built and instrumented, the two open guardrail PRs are merged, dev tags are pinned, /health endpoints are added to modern-core, modern-core-db and postgres, and the notification outbox capacity is hardened against the 500-transaction spike. If those preconditions cannot be met this quarter, the pilot slips with them; it does not launch into a known breaking point.

**Next officer to direct:** The **CTO**, because the preconditions are engineering gaps the CTO already owns — the scheduler build, the open guardrail PRs, the dev-tag pinning, the /health instrumentation, and the notification-outbox capacity hardening the COO identified. Once the CTO verifies those items, the pilot ships.
